featured_reviews.name: Mamta Solanki
featured_reviews.review_text:
Circle Wealth Advisors Pvt Ltd develop an overall strategy for our client to meet their needs and goals through an array of Wealth Management service, that includes 3 steps which are Planning, Execution and Monitoring.
At Planning stage, we establish details about your assets and liability, income and expenditure, your relationship with the money, goals and aspirations for the short as well as long term, and also your commitment to meet your objective. After getting the understanding of the data gathered, we create a goal based plan, in which we align your all current investment with your goals and assess if there are any gaps in the current situation. Later, we present our recommendations in the written format which is our action plan.
At Execution stage, we implement the mutually agreed action plan. We will execute the plan only after your consent and not before that.
At Monitoring stage, which is also the most crucial part of the process of wealth management because it is the long term plan and it requires regular quarter as well as annual reviews. Any changes in circumstances, goals, preferences can be inculcated in the plan will during the review. We keep checking returns generated, corpus required for our goal is same, whether the planned goals are relevant or not and any new goals or aspiration being added.
featured_reviews.response_from_owner_text: Thank you Mamta for detailing out the intricate process we follow to meet client expectations and set them on the path of financial independence.

owner_posts.post_text:
At Equalifi's 14th Indian Family Office Summit, Spark Capital PWM was pleased to be part of a session that addressed one of the most consequential — and often overlooked — dimensions of family wealth: the role of women in governance and succession.
 
"Women in Family Business – From Invisible to Indispensable" brought together Arpita Vinay - Senior Managing Director & CEO, Spark Capital PWM, Ritu George Muthoot - Director, Muthoot Pappachan Group, and Aasiya Tejani - Director, Gits Food Products Pvt.Ltd for a candid conversation on how women in India's family enterprises are transitioning from informal influence to formal, decision-making authority.
 
Key themes from the discussion:
 
→ Redefining succession beyond bloodline hierarchy to capability and vision
 → Structuring governance frameworks that reflect the full spectrum of family stakeholders
 → The role of next-generation women in shaping — not just inheriting — family legacy
 → Why inclusive governance is not merely an ethical imperative, but a continuity strategy
 
For family offices, the takeaway is clear: the families best positioned for multi-generational resilience are those that bring every voice — including women — into formal structures with accountability and intention.
 
We thank Equalifi for convening this important conversation, and our panelists for their candour and clarity.

 • Declining crude oil prices and a strengthening rupee are positive macroeconomic developments supporting market sentiment
 • India's structural growth story remains intact, backed by resilient corporate earnings and strong domestic economic fundamentals
 • Domestic liquidity continues to provide stability and support to equity markets amid global uncertainties
 • Maintaining a disciplined and long-term investment approach remains critical for wealth creation through market cycles
 • Select sectors and themes are presenting attractive opportunities for investors willing to look beyond short-term volatility
 
As markets continue to respond to evolving economic and geopolitical developments, periods of correction often create opportunities to accumulate quality businesses at reasonable valuations. Staying focused on fundamentals and long-term value creation remains essential.

A widow walks into a bank to renew a fixed deposit meant for her child’s education. A year later, she discovers she has been sold a life insurance policy — and must pay another large premium or risk losing what she already put in.

This is not just mis-selling. It is a window into a larger problem: high upfront commissions, tax-free maturity proceeds, and a structure where the tax benefit meant for savers have been captured by insurers and the banks acting as their agents.

The real question is uncomfortable: are taxpayers subsidising savers — or Insurance sellers?

My latest Truth Be Told column in Business Standard asks: Who really benefits from tax-free insurance? And if the tax break must continue, should India create a transparent mutual-fund alternative with similar tax concessions, so the benefit finally reaches the saver?

featured_reviews.name: abhishek mishra
featured_reviews.review_text:
**Title:** *Beware – Analah Capital and Fintoo are complete frauds!*

I had a terrible experience with **Analah Capital** through **Fintoo**. I purchased **unlisted Polymatech stocks** from them with the promise and assurance that the company would soon get listed. They portrayed it as a safe and high-potential investment. However, the stock **never got listed**, and I ended up facing a **massive loss of ₹5 lakhs**!

Both Analah Capital and Fintoo completely disappeared when things went wrong — no support, no accountability, and no clear answers. This kind of unethical and misleading behavior is unacceptable. They lure investors with false promises and vanish once they’ve taken your money.

I’m extremely **angry, disappointed, and feel completely cheated** by their false commitments. Please **stay away from Analah Capital and Fintoo** — don’t trust them with your hard-earned money. They are nothing but **fraudsters** in the name of investment advisorsy.
